extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, researchers, and others involved in scholarly publishing and research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and extract evaluation criteria, standards, and recommended practices for journals, peer review, authorship, reproducibility, and identifying predatory journals from a WAME newsletter of publishing news and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabell's blacklist criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabell uses some 65 criteria — which will be reviewed quarterly — to check whether a journal should be on its blacklist, adding points for each suspect finding. Examples include fake editors, plagiarized articles and unclear peer-review policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A team of employees checks for evidence by searching online or contacting authors and journals for verification. Cabell will state all the reasons a journal is on its list, allow publishers/journals to contact Cabell to find out whether they are listed, and provide an opportunity to appeal status once a year. The system is a points-based, periodically-reviewed blacklist intended to limit libel risk by documenting reasons for listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predatory journal characteristics (Beall/Shamseer findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics associated with possibly predatory journals include misspellings, distorted or potentially unauthorized images, editors or editorial board members whose affiliation with the journal was unverified, use of Index Copernicus Value for impact factor, flashy/1990s-style graphics, too many poorly-resized pictures, homepage plastered with logos of indexing services, flashy claimed impact factors, quick publication time, lack of contact address, and spammy 'call for papers' emails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characteristics were empirically associated with journals on Beall’s list but the findings may be circular (overlap with Beall’s criteria) and some characteristics (e.g., stylistic website choices) can falsely identify legitimate journals, particularly those from different cultural/design expectations. Use caution and contextual judgment when applying these markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of predatory behavior beyond website cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational predatory behaviors include accepting fake editors (recruiting unvetted or nonexistent editorial board members), rapid acceptance of submissions (sometimes within hours), appointments contingent on payment, and accepting submissions without proper peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sting operations showed many journals readily accept bogus editor applications or appoint fake editors. Verify editorial board membership, check responsiveness and requirements (e.g., fees) for editorial roles, and confirm peer-review practices rather than relying on surface website features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review — future/innovation recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations for what peer review might look like: find new ways of matching expertise and reviews (including using AI), increase diversity in the reviewer pool (early career researchers, different regions, women), experiment with models that increase transparency, invest in reviewer training, find cross-publisher solutions (e.g., portable peer review), improve recognition for reviewers by funders/institutions/publishers, and use technology to support and enhance the process including automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are practical directions for publishers and platforms to experiment with and implement: improved reviewer identification/verification, training programs, systems for crediting review work, interoperable review portability, and measured trials of transparency models (open review, signed reviews, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: CLUE (Cooperation And Liaison Between Universities And Editors) recommendations for handling suspected misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Main recommendations include creating national registers of individuals/departments responsible for research integrity at institutions; institutions should develop mechanisms for assessing research validity independent from processes to determine whether individual researchers committed misconduct; retain essential research data and peer review records for at least 10 years; and criteria to determine when journals should contact the institution before, or at the same time as, alerting authors in suspected fabrication/falsification cases to prevent destruction of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional CLUE guidance: anonymous or pseudonymous allegations should be judged on merit and not dismissed automatically; institutions should release relevant sections of investigation reports to all journals that published the work under investigation. Editors should define concrete criteria for when to contact institutions rather than always contacting authors first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship standards and contributor-role transparency (NAS & CRediT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards should be based on the principle that those who have made a significant intellectual contribution are authors. Significant contributions include design/conceptualization, conduct of research, analysis/interpretation, or drafting/revising the manuscript. All authors should approve the final manuscript. Standards should identify one or more authors who assume responsibility for the entire work, require disclosure of all author roles and contributions, and specify that gift/honorary authorship, coercive authorship, ghost authorship, and omitting deserving authors are unacceptable. CRediT proposes a contributor roles taxonomy to be embedded in the byline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and societies should develop or adopt disciplinary authorship standards if none exist; embedding a structured taxonomy (e.g., CRediT) helps transparency and accountability. Policies should make responsibility assignment and role disclosure explicit at submission/publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and methodological transparency requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals can improve reproducibility by requiring methodological transparency: detailed methods in the manuscript or supplementary material; public posting of the data behind experiments; and ensuring information sufficient for a knowledgeable person to reproduce results is made available at or soon after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital publishing reduces page-limit constraints — journals should require detailed methods (in main text or supplements) and treat methods posting similarly to data posting. Policies can mandate public availability of data and methods and encourage or require deposition in repositories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer reviewer critical-evaluation checklist (selected items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key questions a reviewer should ask: Can the study design answer the hypothesis posed (e.g., causality claims vs observational design)? Do the conclusions follow from the results or do they exaggerate importance/implications? What are the funding sources and potential conflicts of interest of the authors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is part of a broader set (12-question) checklist for reviewers. Reviewers should assess design–hypothesis fit, logical consistency between results and claims, and transparency about funding and COI; add discipline-specific checks as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical reporting and transparency standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should require exact sample sizes (not intervals or vague statements), clear attribution of which statistical test was used for which figure or table (including post-hoc tests after ANOVA), disclosure of all statistical tests carried out including negative findings, and where appropriate, power analyses and sample-size calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous sample-size reporting (e.g., 'n = 3–18', 'n > 3', 'data representative of 3 rats from 2 independent experiments') obstructs reproducibility. Editors should demand precise sample counts and explicit mapping of statistical tests to results displays; statistical reviewers or biostatisticians may be necessary for complex analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal standards: ORCID adoption and integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Consortia and journals should encourage or require ORCID identifiers, integrating ORCID iDs into manuscript submission systems, grant application processes, and membership databases to improve author identification and workflow integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consortia members may use API access to integrate ORCID across systems; journals can mandate or strongly encourage ORCID iDs at submission to aid disambiguation and contributor tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical image screening for manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals are hiring technical image editors to manually screen images for potential manipulation or duplication prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manual screening complements automated checks. Journals should consider dedicated staff or contracted services to examine images for manipulation, duplication, and reuse issues as part of pre-publication checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review (PPPR) best practices and success metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: PPPR should compile comments with the article so readers see the post-publication discussion; success has been measured as the percentage of papers with comments, but value may also be judged by whether comments are useful to commenters, some readers, and possibly authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals/platforms should integrate PPPR content with the article record, consider metrics beyond raw comment counts (e.g., substantive corrections triggered), and accept that PPPR may be valuable even if used by a minority of readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of good citation/performance indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: A good indicator simplifies underlying data, is reliable in reporting, provides transparency to the underlying data, is difficult to game, and has a tight theoretical connection to the underlying construct it attempts to measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing or designing metrics (e.g., impact measures), prefer indicators that are theoretically justified, transparent about the data sources and calculations, robust to manipulation, and interpretable in relation to the construct of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest (COI) handling guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure is useful as a minimum expectation but fundamentally insufficient; COI should be mitigated with additional strategies. For guideline-development panels, acceptability of recommendations requires a clear explanation linking evidence to recommendations and balancing harms and benefits. Journals should have policies on how editors handle their own COIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and journals need mitigation tools beyond disclosure (recusal, external review, transparent justification). Small journals with few decision-makers may need alternative solutions. COI policies should be tailored to panel/guideline contexts and to editorial governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial Expressions of Concern (EEoC) use and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: EEoCs have been issued for concerns mainly about validity of data, methods, or interpretation (68%); image issues affected 40% of publications with EEoCs. Some EEoCs have been removed by publishers without leaving a record, and some were not submitted for PubMed/PMC indexing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should maintain transparent records of EEoCs, index them reliably, and ensure an auditable trail. The prevalence of validity and image concerns highlights the need for clear procedures and documentation when issuing EEoCs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer and reviewer-account verification to prevent fake peer review and misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake peer-review incidents (and reviewers stealing authors' data) indicate the need to verify reviewer identities, affiliations, and potential conflicts; also to guard against reviewers exploiting access to unpublished manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial offices should validate reviewer email addresses/affiliations, avoid relying solely on author-suggested reviewers without independent checks, monitor for suspiciously rapid or uniformly positive reviews, and put safeguards (audit trails, reviewer training, and verification technologies) in place to reduce fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling research-misconduct investigations and protecting whistleblowers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whistleblowers need internationally accepted codes of conduct during investigations, including rules such as not attacking scientists in public while investigations run, no personal insults, and no mass e-mails intended to ruin reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and institutions should adopt policies protecting confidentiality and fair process during investigations; have clear communication channels and criteria to determine when to involve institutions vs authors; provide protections for both whistleblowers and accused parties until investigations conclude.
